title: Environments and packages
subtitle: pip, venv, pyproject and a project layout that scales
goal: Set up isolated Python projects with venv and pip, pin dependencies, lay out a project professionally, and reason about versions in code.
outcomes: Explain how pip installs packages from PyPI, and where they go
Create, activate and recreate a virtual environment for each project
Pin dependencies in requirements.txt and describe a project in pyproject.toml
Lay out a project with src/ and tests/ and track it with git
Parse requirement lines and compare version numbers correctly in Python

slides.title: Mission 39: Ship-ready projects
slides.body: Real projects stand on other people's code: web frameworks, data libraries, API clients. Today you learn to install it **safely and reproducibly**, so *"works on my machine"* becomes *"works on every machine"*.

lines: Successfully installed certifi-2024.8.30 charset-normalizer-3.4.0 idna-3.10 requests-2.32.3 urllib3-2.2.3

slides.say: Real projects stand on the shoulders of other people's code: web frameworks, data libraries, API clients. Today you learn how to install that code safely, keep each project separate, and describe your project so that works on my machine becomes works on every machine. These are the commands you will type on day one of any Python job.

slides.title: How pip and PyPI work
slides.body:
**PyPI** (pypi.org) hosts 500,000+ open-source packages. **pip** downloads a package and its dependencies into the active Python's `site-packages` folder.

Only install packages you trust: attackers publish look-alike names (*typosquatting*).

items: pip asks pypi.org for the latest matching version
downloads a wheel (.whl) plus its dependencies
installs them into site-packages of the active Python

slides.say: PyPI, the Python Package Index, hosts more than half a million open source packages. When you type pip install requests, pip asks PyPI for the package, downloads a ready-built file called a wheel, installs its dependencies too, and puts everything into the site packages folder of whichever Python is active. One warning: attackers publish packages with names one letter away from popular ones, so check the spelling.

slides.title: Which Python am I running?
slides.code:
import sys

print(sys.version_info.major, sys.version_info.minor)
print(sys.version_info >= (3, 10))

in_venv = sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix
print("inside a virtual environment:", in_venv)
slides.expect:
3 13
True
inside a virtual environment: False
explain: In a venv, prefix is the .venv folder; base_prefix is the real Python.
slides.say: Your code can ask which Python is running it. Version info compares like a tuple, which is how libraries check that you have a new enough Python. And here is a neat trick: inside a virtual environment, sys dot prefix points to the environment's folder, while base prefix still points to the original Python. On your laptop, run this inside and outside a venv and watch the last line change.

slides.title: Why virtual environments?
slides.body: All projects share **one** global `site-packages`, but your shop API needs Django 5 and an old blog needs Django 4. A **virtual environment** (`venv`) gives each project its own private folder of packages.
slides.say: Without virtual environments, every project on your laptop shares one folder of packages. Then one project needs Django five, another needs Django four, and upgrading one breaks the other. A virtual environment gives each project its own private Python and its own packages, in a folder usually called dot venv. Professionals create one for every project, without exception.

slides.title: The venv workflow
slides.body: `.venv/` is disposable: never commit it. Anyone can rebuild it from `requirements.txt`.
slides.say: Here is the routine. Create the environment once with python dash m venv. Activate it, and your prompt shows its name, so pip and python now point inside it. Install the project's dependencies from its requirements file, run your tests, and deactivate when you are done. On Windows the activate script lives in a Scripts folder instead.

slides.title: Recreate the environment
slides.q: A teammate clones your repository. What do they need to recreate your exact environment?
options: requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml), then pip install inside a fresh venv
Nothing: pip remembers what you installed
slides.why: A .venv contains machine-specific paths and binaries, so it doesn't travel. The dependency list does: a new venv plus pip install -r requirements.txt rebuilds it anywhere.
slides.say: Quick check. A new teammate clones your project. What do they need from you to rebuild the same environment?

slides.title: requirements.txt and version pins
slides.body:
Versions follow **MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH** (semantic versioning): a major bump may break your code.

**Pin** exact versions for apps you deploy, so a surprise upgrade can't break production on a Friday night.
slides.say: Most packages use semantic versioning: major, minor, patch. A patch fixes bugs, a minor version adds features, and a new major version may break your code. A requirements file lists what to install, with a specifier for each package. For an app you deploy, pin exact versions with double equals, so a surprise upgrade can never break production on a Friday night.

slides.title: Read a requirements file
slides.expect:
requests       pinned to 2.32.3
flask          pinned to 3.0.3
pandas>=2.2    NOT pinned
python-dotenv  NOT pinned

files.requirements.txt:
# web
requests==2.32.3
flask==3.0.3

pandas>=2.2   # analytics
python-dotenv

explain: The file sits next to main.py.
Blank lines are skipped with a guard.
slides.say: A requirements file is just text, so Python can audit it. We read the file line by line, drop comments, skip blank lines, and report which packages are pinned. Two of them are not. In a real team, a check like this runs automatically and warns before anything gets deployed.

slides.title: Predict: comparing versions
slides.why: Strings compare character by character: '1' < '9', so "3.10" < "3.9". Tuples of ints compare number by number: 10 > 9. Never compare versions as strings.
slides.say: Python three point ten is newer than three point nine. But what does Python say when you compare them as strings, and as tuples of numbers?

slides.title: Compare versions properly
slides.code:
def parse_version(text):
    return tuple(int(part) for part in text.split("."))

installed = "2.31.0"
required = "2.32"

print(parse_version(installed))
print(parse_version(installed) >= parse_version(required))

versions = ["1.10.0", "1.2.9", "1.9.3", "1.10.1"]
print(sorted(versions))
print(sorted(versions, key=parse_version))
slides.say: Turn each version into a tuple of integers and comparisons become correct. Two point thirty one is older than two point thirty two, so this environment needs an upgrade. Sorting as text puts one point ten before one point two, which is wrong. Sorting with parse version as the key gets it right. Real tools use the packaging library, which also understands versions like two point zero r c one.

slides.title: pyproject.toml: one file to describe it all
slides.body: Modern projects describe themselves in **pyproject.toml**: name, version, Python version, dependencies, and settings for tools like ruff and pytest. Tools such as `pip`, `uv` and `poetry` read it.

visual.verdict: pyproject.toml says what the project needs; pinned files say exactly what gets installed.

slides.say: Modern Python projects describe themselves in one file called pyproject dot toml. It holds the project's name and version, which Python versions it supports, its dependencies, and settings for tools like ruff and pytest. Pip, uv and poetry all read it. A common pattern: pyproject lists flexible ranges, and a lock or requirements file pins exact versions for deployment.

slides.title: Read pyproject.toml with tomllib
slides.code:
import tomllib

with open("pyproject.toml", "rb") as f:
    config = tomllib.load(f)

project = config["project"]
print(project["name"], project["version"])
print("needs Python", project["requires-python"])
for dep in project["dependencies"]:
    print("-", dep)
print("dev tools:", project["optional-dependencies"]["dev"])
print("ruff line length:", config["tool"]["ruff"]["line-length"])
slides.expect:
chai-tracker 0.1.0
needs Python >=3.11
- requests>=2.31
- rich~=13.7
dev tools: ['pytest>=8', 'ruff']
ruff line length: 100

files.pyproject.toml:
[project]
name = "chai-tracker"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Track your daily chai, with charts"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
dependencies = [
    "requests>=2.31",
    "rich~=13.7",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff"]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100

explain: tomllib needs the file opened in binary mode: rb.
TOML becomes nested dicts and lists.
Optional extras, installed with pip install -e ".[dev]".
slides.say: TOML is a simple configuration format, and since Python three eleven the standard library can read it with tomllib. The file opens in binary mode, and load turns it into ordinary dictionaries and lists. This is exactly how tools like ruff find their settings in your project.

slides.title: A project layout that scales
slides.body:
- `src/<package>/`: your importable code
- `tests/`: tests that mirror the package
- `pyproject.toml`, `README.md`, `.gitignore` at the root

The `src/` folder stops tests from accidentally importing the uninstalled copy.
slides.say: Here is the layout most professional Python projects use. Your code lives in a package inside a src folder, and tests live in a separate tests folder that mirrors it. Configuration and the readme sit at the root. The src folder looks like extra ceremony, but it guarantees your tests run against the installed package, exactly as your users will.

slides.title: A package of your own
slides.body: A **package** is a folder with `__init__.py`. Here: `chai_tracker/__init__.py` and `chai_tracker/core.py`.
slides.code:
import chai_tracker
from chai_tracker.core import cups_today

print(chai_tracker.__version__)
print(cups_today({"morning": 2, "evening": 1}))
print(chai_tracker.cups_today is cups_today)
explain: Import from a module inside the package.
__init__ re-exported it: the same function object.
slides.say: A package is a folder with an init file. This one has a core module, and its init file re-exports the main function and sets a version string. So users can import the function from the package directly, and both names point to the very same function object. Open the files tab to see the two files.

slides.title: git for Python projects
slides.body: Commit your **code, tests, pyproject.toml and requirements**. Never commit `.venv/`, `__pycache__/` or `.env` files with secrets: list them in `.gitignore`.
slides.say: Every professional project lives in git. Start with git init, then create a dot gitignore file that keeps out the virtual environment, Python's cache folders, and any dot env file with passwords or API keys. Then add and commit. Small commits with clear messages make your history a story your teammates can follow.

slides.title: Ask what's installed: importlib.metadata
slides.expect:
requests -> not installed
flask -> not installed
explain: Standard library: reads installed packages' metadata.
Not installed? Return None instead of crashing.
slides.say: Your program can ask which packages are installed, and at which version, using importlib dot metadata. On your laptop, inside a venv with requests installed, this prints its version number. In this phone's Python, neither package is installed, and our function handles that gracefully instead of crashing.

slides.title: Parse a requirements file
slides.task:
Write `parse_requirements(text)` that returns a list of `(name, operator, version)` tuples.

- skip blank lines and `#` comments (whole-line and inline)
- names in lower case
- operators: `==`, `>=`, `<=`, `~=`, `!=`, `>`, `<`, with optional spaces
- no version: `(name, None, None)`
slides.starter:
def parse_requirements(text):
    # TODO: return a list of (name, operator, version) tuples
    return []

sample = """# web
requests==2.32.3
Flask>=3.0  # web framework

python-dotenv
"""
print(parse_requirements(sample))
slides.solution:
OPERATORS = ["==", ">=", "<=", "~=", "!=", ">", "<"]   # two-character ones first

def parse_requirements(text):
    result = []
    for line in text.splitlines():
        line = line.split("#")[0].strip()
        if not line:
            continue
        for op in OPERATORS:
            if op in line:
                name, version = line.split(op, 1)
                result.append((name.strip().lower(), op, version.strip()))
                break
        else:
            result.append((line.lower(), None, None))
    return result

sample = """# web
requests==2.32.3
Flask>=3.0  # web framework

python-dotenv
"""
print(parse_requirements(sample))
slides.tests:
text = "# web
requests==2.32.3
Flask>=3.0  # web framework

python-dotenv
numpy == 2.1.0
rich~=13.7
"
got = parse_requirements(text)
want = [("requests", "==", "2.32.3"), ("flask", ">=", "3.0"), ("python-dotenv", None, None), ("numpy", "==", "2.1.0"), ("rich", "~=", "13.7")]
for i, w in enumerate(want):
    assert i < len(got), f"Expected {len(want)} requirements, got {len(got)}: {got}"
    assert tuple(got[i]) == w, f"Line {i + 1} should parse to {w}, got {got[i]}."
assert len(got) == len(want), f"Expected exactly {len(want)} requirements, got {len(got)}. Skip blank lines and comments."
assert parse_requirements("") == [], "Empty text gives an empty list."
assert parse_requirements("# only comments
   
") == [], "Only comments and blank lines: return []."
hints: Clean each line first: line.split("#")[0].strip(), and skip it if empty.
Find the operator: loop over ["==", ">=", "<=", "~=", "!=", ">", "<"] (two-character ones first) and use the first one that appears in the line.
Then name, version = line.split(op, 1), strip both and lower-case the name. No operator at all? Append (line.lower(), None, None): a for...else is perfect here.
slides.say: Dependency tools all start by parsing requirement lines. Write parse requirements, which turns a requirements file into a list of tuples of name, operator and version. Skip comments and blank lines, lower case the names, and allow spaces around the operator. Plain string methods are enough, which is a good reminder that not every text problem needs a regex.

slides.title: Check the environment
slides.task:
Write `outdated(required, installed)`. Both are dicts of `name → version`. `required` holds **minimum** versions. Return a list sorted by name with:

- `"pandas: missing"` when not installed
- `"requests: 2.31.0 < 2.32"` when too old

Compare numerically, and treat `3.0` and `3.0.0` as equal.
slides.tests:
req = {"requests": "2.32", "flask": "3.0.0", "rich": "13.7", "pandas": "2.2"}
inst = {"requests": "2.31.0", "flask": "3.0", "rich": "13.10.1"}
got = outdated(req, inst)
assert "pandas: missing" in got, f"pandas isn't installed, so expect 'pandas: missing' in {got}."
assert "requests: 2.31.0 < 2.32" in got, f"requests 2.31.0 is older than 2.32: expect 'requests: 2.31.0 < 2.32' in {got}."
assert not any(m.startswith("rich") for m in got), "rich 13.10.1 is NEWER than 13.7: compare numbers, not strings."
assert not any(m.startswith("flask") for m in got), "flask 3.0 and 3.0.0 are the same version: pad the shorter tuple with zeros."
assert got == ["pandas: missing", "requests: 2.31.0 < 2.32"], f"Sort the messages by package name. Got {got}."
assert outdated({}, {"x": "1.0"}) == [], "Nothing required: no problems."
assert outdated({"django": "4.2"}, {"django": "5.1"}) == [], "django 5.1 satisfies a minimum of 4.2."
hints: Loop over sorted(required). Use installed.get(name) to spot missing packages.
Compare parse_version(have) < parse_version(need), not the strings.
Before comparing, pad the shorter tuple: a += (0,) * (width - len(a)).
slides.say: Before deploying, teams check that every dependency is installed and new enough. Write outdated, which compares required minimum versions with what is installed. Watch out for two traps: thirteen point ten is newer than thirteen point seven, and three point zero equals three point zero point zero.

slides.title: What goes into git?
slides.q: Which of these belongs in your project's git repository?
slides.why: Commit what others need to rebuild and run the project. .venv and __pycache__ are generated on each machine, and .env holds secrets that must never be pushed.
slides.say: Last check. Of these four, which one should you actually commit to your repository?

slides.title: Mission 39 complete
points: pip installs packages from PyPI into the active Python's site-packages
One venv per project: python -m venv .venv, activate, pip install -r requirements.txt
Pin exact versions for apps; semantic versions are MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
pyproject.toml describes the project; src/ and tests/ keep the layout clean
Compare versions as tuples of ints, never as strings; commit code and config, not .venv or secrets
slides.say: Mission thirty nine complete. You can set up isolated environments, pin dependencies, describe a project with pyproject, lay it out like a professional, and compare versions correctly in code.
